stories.title: Analysis: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small swears in its reasoning traces
stories.summary: Vals AI found Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small model cursed 316 times across 2,655 benchmark runs, mostly late in failing runs, though 96% of failed runs showed no profanity at all.
stories.more: The analysis, conducted by Vals AI, examined the internal reasoning text generated by Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small model across 2,655 benchmark runs. It counted 316 instances of profanity, concentrated late in long reasoning sequences that ultimately failed. Despite this pattern, the correlation is weak as a predictor of failure: 96 percent of failed runs contained no cursing at all. The findings suggest the swearing is a curiosity in the model's reasoning rather than a reliable warning sign of an impending failed run.

items.title: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs
items.excerpt: Thinking Machines' AI model Inkling 2 Small swears during its internal reasoning, 316 times across 2,655 benchmark runs, according to an analysis by Vals AI. The profanity typically shows up late in long runs that fail anyway. But it doesn't work as a warning signal: 96 percent of failed runs contained no cursing at all. The article Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs appeared first on The Decoder .

stories.title: Vals AI benchmark: open models narrow the gap on cyberattack skill
stories.summary: A Vals AI benchmark finds OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol Daybreak hits 80.8% of simulated attack objectives, while open-weight DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reaches 72.8% at a tenth of the cost, narrowing the gap.
stories.more: In Vals AI's benchmark of simulated attacks on corporate networks, OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol Daybreak achieved an 80.8 percent success rate on attack objectives. The open-weight DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reached 72.8 percent at roughly a tenth of the cost of the closed model. Analysts cited in the coverage say that because open-weight models' capabilities cannot be restricted after release, the practical window for defenders to prepare is narrowing. The benchmark results for other models in the comparison were not detailed in the excerpt.

items.title: The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking
items.excerpt: In the Vals AI benchmark, OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol Daybreak hits 80.8 percent of attack objectives in simulated corporate networks. Worse, the open-weight model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reaches 72.8 percent at a tenth of the cost. Because open models can no longer be restricted, analysts say the window for defenders is shrinking fast. The article The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking appeared first on The Decoder .

stories.title: Nous Research strips pro-China bias from Qwen3.8-27B via fine-tuning
stories.summary: Nous Research retrained Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B into Arete-27B, cutting pro-Chinese propaganda responses from 22% to under 1% using 53 million tokens of fine-tuning, with capabilities intact.
stories.more: Nous Research used 53 million tokens of supervised fine-tuning to retrain Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B into a new model it calls Arete-27B. The rate of pro-Chinese propaganda in test responses dropped from 22 percent to under 1 percent after retraining, while general capabilities reportedly remained intact. The team describes the political bias in the base model as being 'applied late' and 'thin,' sitting on top of the model rather than embedded deeply in it. The result suggests such biases in some open-weight Chinese models can be substantially reduced with comparatively modest fine-tuning effort.

items.title: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away
items.excerpt: Nous Research retrained Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to produce Arete-27B, largely stripping out its pro-Chinese bias. The propaganda rate dropped from 22 percent to less than one percent, while general capabilities remained intact in tests. The method relied on 53 million tokens of supervised fine-tuning. The political bias is "applied late, it is applied thin," the team writes. stories.title: Uncensored DeepSeek V4 Pro / Qwen3.5 9B distillation trends on Hugging Face
stories.summary: A community-made, uncensored distillation combining DeepSeek V4 Pro and Qwen3.5 reasoning, published by user xtools-at, became a top-trending model on Hugging Face with 360 likes and over 1,300 downloads.
stories.more: The model, published under the name 'heretic' by Hugging Face user xtools-at, is tagged as a distillation combining DeepSeek and Qwen3.5-based architectures. Its listed tags indicate it was trained using supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and GSPO, built with the Unsloth training framework. It is categorized for text generation, with image-text-to-text also among its tags. As of trending, it had 360 likes and 1,369 downloads, with no further benchmark or model card details available in the listing.

stories.title: NYT: Nvidia-approved Chinese chip buyer's office found empty
stories.summary: The New York Times reports that New Matrix, a Chinese firm cleared to receive Nvidia H200 chips under US export rules, operates from an apparently empty office, raising questions about vetting.
stories.more: According to The New York Times, New Matrix appears on the US government's list of Chinese firms approved to handle Nvidia's export-controlled H200 AI chips. Visits to the company's registered address reportedly found empty offices, described as a 'hollow gray shell.' The finding has raised concerns that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia adequately vetted the firm before clearing it to receive the hardware. It remains unclear whether New Matrix has actually received any chips or what follow-up review, if any, is planned.

stories.title: Verge podcast: Cognition's Alex Stamos on AI upending cybersecurity
stories.summary: In the first episode of a new Verge series on AI in real life, Cognition chief security officer Alex Stamos discusses how AI has disrupted the cybersecurity landscape.
stories.more: The episode features Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and a longtime cybersecurity figure, in conversation with The Verge. It is billed as part one of a special series examining AI's real-world effects, starting with cybersecurity. The excerpt frames the current state of cybersecurity as chaotic but does not detail specific attacks, incidents, or defensive measures discussed in the episode. Further installments of the series are expected to cover other areas of AI in real life.

stories.title: METR report: Anthropic's AI-assisted AI development is accelerating fast
stories.summary: A METR report following an 11-week investigation finds Anthropic is using AI to build AI roughly twice as fast as a year ago with little sign of slowing, alarming safety researchers.
stories.more: The report was published by METR, an AI safety research organization, after an 11-week investigation into how Anthropic develops its own models. It concludes that Anthropic's use of AI to accelerate internal AI development is working well, with the pace of improvement roughly double what it was a year earlier. The report notes little indication that this acceleration is slowing down. The Verge describes the trend as alarming to researchers, though the excerpt does not specify which particular risks concern them most.

stories.title: NYT Cooking's AI assistant helps weeknight dinner, flubs a cake
stories.summary: A Verge writer's first-person review of NYT Cooking's AI recipe assistant found it useful for picking weeknight dinners but says it nearly ruined a cake, pointing to uneven reliability.
stories.more: The piece is a first-person account from a writer who regularly struggles to decide on weeknight dinners beyond repeating chicken dishes. They describe trying NYT Cooking's AI assistant for meal planning and finding it helpful for that weeknight decision. The same assistant reportedly gave guidance that nearly ruined a cake when applied to baking. The excerpt does not detail what specifically went wrong with the cake or how the assistant's recommendations differed between the two uses.
